Emulator sites vary, but for software you can check out Retroarch by Libreto. It's an open source, all-in-one emulator that runs on most platforms and mounts an emulator core for each system you want to emulate. You set the control layout once and it carries across all cores. Xbox controllers should be plug and play.

If you're looking to make a dedicated retro emulation box, you can try "Lakka", Retroarch's official Linux distribution. Load it on a mini-pc, plug in a controller and you've got a dedicated retro emulation box.
Any game that you bought for the old game consoles can be legally backed up for your own use. If you would like more info on ROMs PM me.

You're not going to find much as far as free games go, legally. I know that some of the old Home PCs have had their libraries somewhat "freed", but certainly not officially. As far as standard consoles go on the other hand, it's pretty much all stuff that still has active copyright holders.

Regardless, since there's nothing illegal about emulators itself, /emugen/'s website has by far the best listing of them.

For emulators, you'll want Retroarch (for Anything on nearly anything) or Bizhawk (for PC). RA is more time consuming to get all set up at first, but supports emulating more systems and more host systems then than Bizhawk. Most recommend RA above Bizhawk for general purpose emulation, but Bizhawk is the best multi-system emu I've found other than RA and is more than sufficent.

As for ROMs, Google is more than sufficent to find whatever you want. A few tips to stay safe while hunting:

  • Don't ever open an executable (.exe) thinking it's a ROM; it isn't. Roms come in a specific standard format/extension for each system and you should only open these file types using your chosen emulator.
    (i.e. .nes file for NES, .gb/c for Gamboy/Color, .nds for DS, .iso for PSX/PS2, etc.)
  • When you download a ROM, it will either be the proper format (.nes) or an archive (.zip, .rar, .7z). If it is either of the latter 2 archive formats, I recommend 7-zip to extract it until you get the proper file format.
  • Use an ad blocker. Most ROM sites use ad networks that are not stringent about what appears in the ads so fake download links are dirt common.

The only ROM that I can directly point you to under rule 6 is D-Pad Hero, a pair of NES homebrew games inspired by classic video game music and Guitar Hero. These'll work fine to test your emulators before you go hunting for old-school commercial ROMs.

I recommend you either shell out for an older console (some of these go seriously cheap, especially if you look in charity shops and boot sales) and then buy some games for it (usually also rather cheap). If you don't have the money, emulate, but I SERIOUSLY recommend you don't emulate past nintendo 64's generation. Even nintendo 64 emulators are seriously bad in terms of fidelity (glitches, sound, picture) compared to the real thing. If you end up really liking retro games, then I don't think you should spoil your first impressions of them using an inferior emulation.

What do I recommend if you don't have the money to buy an old console? Anything SNES and below. The SNES in particular has a really amazing range of games, although so too does the NES, Sega Genesis etc.

Is there any specific reason incorporating Voat was actually necessary to continue functioning?

I would assume the same reason that most corporations exist - limited liability.

A corporation is a legal fiction - for all legal purposes, it's treated as an individual in and of itself, so if, for instance, some crusading busybody wanted to file a suit against Voat for hosting harassing content, she could only sue the corporation. If the corporation didn't exist, she could sue the owners individually.

For a forum that holds to a principle of freedom of speech, I would say that incorporation is definitely necessary, since there are so many people (and governments) in the world that want to attack that freedom, and those who defend it. This way, they can only target the corporation itself.
